title: Space Apps Challenge: Health Monitoring Software Overview
text:
Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health. With rising investment in spacecraft technology and research, space missions have become more ambitious. NASA’s Artemis program recently accomplished a crewed lunar flyby, and NASA and others have plans to send humans to Mars in the future. With increasingly longer missions, astronauts will be more exposed to the hostile space environment, which brings both physical and mental health risks.

NASA’s Human Research Program has mapped the five hazards of human spaceflight, which are space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. These hazards can contribute to health problems such as immune system changes, bone density loss, cardiovascular events, inadequate nutrition, behavioral health conditions, and others. Astronauts must be capable of making health assessments on themselves during a mission, to prevent and treat health problems that may arise. Some useful health indicators are blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, daily sleep hours, and mood.

title: Space Apps Challenge: Objectives and Design Considerations
text:
Your challenge is to create a visual tool that helps astronauts assess their own health during space missions and provides guidance on treatments and health improvements. You may consider gathering data from the user through any kind of input—keyboard text, mouse clicks, or camera images, for example. Any kind of data can be used, as long as it represents a health indicator, such as blood sugar levels in mg/dL or ultrasound images.

You can use NASA’s Human Research Program resources, along with the publicly available resources from other space agencies, to understand how spaceflight hazards affect human health, and to decide which indicators are useful and how they can support a quick assessment. Which measurements can be performed in space? Why is an exam needed? How do spaceflight hazards affect these health indicators? When might a result warrant attention from the crew or from flight surgeons on the ground? What actions can be taken to prevent a critical health condition? These are questions worth considering as you develop your solution.

User interface design plays an important role in presenting metrics and diagnosis clearly. You may consider taking advantage of animations and interactivity to present the information. For example, the software could display a human figure where each part of the body is clickable and displays information about its function and health status. Considerations: Your tool could provide health insights for astronauts in different environments, such as a spacecraft, a space station, a rover, or a base on another planet or moon. Your tool could prompt astronauts to take measurements or complete specific actions from time to time as a part of the mission routine. Your tool could include a gamification system to help astronauts engage with tasks that support their health. Your tool could include dynamic charts that show how astronaut’s health indicators change over time. Your tool could include color coding that helps the astronaut interpret the status of a health indicator at a glance. Do not assume that astronauts know everything about how to assess their health. Your tool could provide simple instructions and explanations covering measurements, health indicators, and risks.

title: Hazard 1: Space Radiation Biology and Monitoring
text: Hazard: Space Radiation. Mechanism: Beyond Earth's protective atmosphere and magnetosphere, astronauts are bombarded by ionizing radiation, primarily Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR - high-energy atomic nuclei) and Solar Particle Events (SPE - energetic protons from solar flares). Physiological Effects: Increased lifetime risk of radiation-induced carcinogenesis (leukemia, solid tumors); Central Nervous System (CNS) alterations: cognitive impairment, executive function deficits, neuro-inflammation; Degenerative cardiovascular disease and endothelial tissue damage; Acute Radiation Sickness (ARS) risk during severe, unshielded SPEs (nausea, vomiting, immune collapse) Monitoring: Personal radiation dosimeters (accumulated dose in mSv); Real-time dose rate (mSv/hr or microGy/hr); Neutron fraction detection (e.g., CANS instrument); Biomarkers: DNA double-strand break repair indicators, complete blood counts (lymphocytes) Countermeasures: Storm shelters within deep-space transit vehicles; Hydrogen-rich active/passive shielding (polyethylene, water walls); Radioprotective pharmaceuticals and antioxidant supplementation; Mission duration limits based on career permissible exposure limits (PEL)

title: Hazard 2: Isolation and Confinement Behavioral Health
text: Hazard: Isolation and Confinement. Mechanism: Small multi-cultural crews residing in cramped, high-workload habitats for months to years, cut off from terrestrial social contact, natural diurnal light cycles, and familiar environments. Physiological Effects: Behavioral health decline: depression, anxiety, chronic situational stress; Circadian desynchronization and chronic sleep debt (<6 hours/night); Interpersonal tension, communication breakdowns, and psychological friction; Decreased alertness, cognitive processing speed, and situational awareness Monitoring: Daily sleep duration (hours) and sleep architecture (REM/deep sleep via actigraphy); Daily subjective mood rating (e.g., scale 1-10 or multidimensional mood score); Cognitive assessment battery scores (reaction time, working memory); Voice/speech acoustic stress analysis and facial expression metrics Countermeasures: Circadian-aligned dynamic habitat lighting (blue-enriched morning light); Structured private communication with family and ground psychological support; Gamified psychological decompression and behavioral self-help software; Routine schedules balancing exercise, duties, and off-duty recreation

title: Hazard 3: Distance from Earth and Clinical Autonomy
text: Hazard: Distance from Earth. Mechanism: Transit to deep space (Moon ~240,000 miles; Mars ~140 million miles average). Communication latency increases up to 20-22 minutes each way for Mars, making real-time ground guidance impossible. Evacuation/resupply impossible. Physiological Effects: Inability to evacuate ill or injured crew members to terrestrial emergency rooms; Exacerbation of acute medical events (appendicitis, sepsis, toxic exposure, fractures); Heightened psychological burden on crew who must act as primary caregivers and flight surgeons Monitoring: Autonomous onboard medical checklist completion logs; Consumable medical kit inventory tracking (pharmaceutical expiration, surgical tools); Automated diagnostic sensor readings (ECG, ultrasound, point-of-care blood chemistry); Clinical decision support system (CDSS) diagnostic confidence scores Countermeasures: Autonomous AI clinical decision support tools providing step-by-step diagnostic workflows; Point-of-care laboratory devices (i-STAT, compact hematology analyzers); Cross-training crew members in emergency medical procedures and minor surgery; Rigorous telemedicine protocols optimized for store-and-forward communication

title: Hazard 4: Gravity Fields, Microgravity Deconditioning, and SANS
text: Hazard: Gravity Fields (Altered Gravity). Mechanism: Transitions through three gravitational states: 1G (Earth) -> 0G (Microgravity in transit) -> 0.16G (Lunar surface) / 0.38G (Martian surface) -> 1G return. Physiological Effects: Bone mineral density loss: 1% to 1.5% loss per month in load-bearing bones (femur, spine, pelvis); Muscle atrophy: loss of muscle mass, volume, and peak power, particularly in slow-twitch postural muscles; Cephalad fluid shift: ~2 liters of blood and interstitial fluid shift toward the chest and head, causing facial puffiness, nasal congestion, and decreased total plasma volume; Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS): optic disc edema, posterior globe flattening, hyperopic shift, and choroidal folds; Cardiovascular deconditioning and orthostatic intolerance upon return to gravity (dizziness, fainting); Vestibular disorientation and Space Motion Sickness (SMS) during initial 48-72 hours Monitoring: Blood pressure (systolic/diastolic mmHg, supine and standing/loaded); Heart rate (resting, peak exercise bpm); Body mass / weight tracking (using inertial acceleration mass measurement devices); Ultrasound imaging: optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD), cardiac ventricular volume; Muscle strength / dynamometry and jump power metrics Countermeasures: 2 to 2.5 hours of daily intense resistive and aerobic exercise (ARED, T2 treadmill, CEVIS cycle ergometer); Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) suits to draw fluids back to lower extremities; Fluid and electrolyte replenishment prior to gravitational re-entry; Compression garments (anti-g suits) for re-entry and post-landing mobility

title: Hazard 5: Hostile Closed Environments and ECLSS Monitoring
text: Hazard: Hostile Closed Environments. Mechanism: An engineered life-support habitat recycling 100% of air and water, with restricted volume, artificial atmospheric pressure and gas mixtures, continuous equipment acoustic noise, and altered microbial biomes. Physiological Effects: Hypercapnia symptoms from localized carbon dioxide pockets (>3-5 mmHg CO2): headaches, lethargy, mental fog; Immune dysregulation: suppression of T-cell function and reactivation of latent herpesviruses (EBV, VZV); Microbiome shifts and microbial proliferation in humid crevices, filters, and surfaces; Toxic inhalation risks from off-gassing synthetic polymers or chemical coolant leaks (e.g., ammonia); Acoustic trauma and temporary threshold shifts from continuous environmental ECLSS fans/pumps Monitoring: Ambient cabin CO2 partial pressure (mmHg) and total cabin pressure (psi / kPa); Pulse Oximetry (SpO2 %); Core body temperature (°C / °F) to detect early microbial infection; Cabin acoustic sound levels (dB); Air and water microbial sample counts (CFU/m3, CFU/100mL) Countermeasures: Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) with catalytic oxidizers and CO2 scrubbers; High-Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) and microbial air filters; Regular habitat surface wiping with antimicrobial disinfectants; Strict materials qualification avoiding toxic volatile organic compound (VOC) off-gassing

title: CSA: CANS Instrument and Neutron Radiation on ISS
text:
Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health. Radiation is one of the key challenges faced by astronauts living and working beyond the protective shield of Earth’s atmosphere. As Canada and its international partners advance plans for missions to the Moon, and eventually Mars, the CSA continues to invest in technology to better understand exposure levels.

The CSA has awarded a contract of $5.5 million to Bubble Technology Industries for the continued development of the CANS, a compact and autonomous instrument designed to measure neutron radiation exposure in space.

Neutron radiation, which contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS, is especially harmful because it can cause serious biological damage and require specialized protective measures. For over 25 years, the ISS has been a test bed for new technology. Canada has significant expertise in radiation detection experiments on the ISS, including MOSFET, EVARM and Radi-N and Radi-N2.

CANS improves upon previous radiation detection methods with the unique combined capabilities of working continuously and autonomously. Data collected could help develop better measures to reduce risks for astronauts’ health and also has potential applications on Earth, including cancer therapy, radiation protection for aircrews, nuclear threat detection and public safety, among others. title: CSA: Science Experiments in Space and Accelerated Aging Analogy
text:
Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?. Science is our quest for more knowledge about the world and ourselves. For thousands of years, humanity has pushed boundaries in its search to learn more about our place in the universe.

Canada's participation in the International Space Station (ISS) allows our scientists to access the unique space environment and conduct cutting-edge experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory to prepare for deep-space destinations and use the knowledge obtained to improve our quality of life on Earth.

Missions to the Moon and Mars mean longer trips and more risks for astronauts, including: more time in weightlessness, more exposure to radiation, longer periods of isolation very far from home, increased delays in communication with Earth, and less ability to rely on Earth for food, materials, and emergency medical assistance.

Studying the way our body changes in space helps us understand the impacts of reduced levels of physical activity and issues that affect older adult populations on Earth. Living in weightless conditions changes the human body in many ways. The effects observed in astronauts are similar to accelerated aging and health problems caused by a sedentary lifestyle. Studying the human body in space for six months gives us data that would take years to gather on Earth. New information gained in space contributes to improved quality of life on Earth.

Canadian scientists use space to study our bones, heart, blood vessels and brain. Their experiments have produced findings that can help people suffering from balance problems, such as seniors; osteoporosis; cardiovascular disorders; and Type-2 diabetes. Why do we do science in space?
2017-11-28 - Did you know that many science experiments are being conducted on the International Space Station at any given time? Why do we do science in space?  (

Canadian Space Agency)
Canadian science on the International Space Station
Transcript
Tim Haltigin:
Hi. I’m Tim. And I like science.
Living in space is a lot tougher on your body than you might think.
Seriously.
Microgravity does a lot of weird stuff to it: your bones and muscles start to deteriorate, blood vessels stiffen, the nervous system is affected, and even your sense of orientation becomes confused.
And of course, all of this is happening as you’re being exposed to higher levels of radiation. Not good!
What’s even worse is that the more time you’re in space, the more pronounced these effects can become.
So as we plan to explore farther out beyond the Earth and eventually fly back to the Moon and even out to Mars, we really need to find ways to minimize these impacts and protect our astronauts’ health.
This is one of the reasons why the International Space Station was built in the first place - to do science!
